name: Targetprocess (Apptio/IBM)
card_surface: Targetprocess goes further than any other tool surveyed in surfacing VCS state directly on the card face. Via Board View Setup > Customize Cards, admins add a dedicated 'DevOps unit' (sometimes called the DevOps section) to any card size (S/M/L/XL). The unit renders a compact block of icons representing aggregated branch and merge/pull-request state: (1) branch indicator showing one or more linked branches, (2) pipeline/CI status icon (success/failed/in-progress, color-coded), (3) approval icon that remains gray until the required number of approvals are received and turns green when met, (4) mergeability alert (an exclamation icon) shown when at least one related MR/PR cannot be merged automatically (conflicts, failed pipeline, or in-progress). Counts can be displayed alongside icons when multiple branches/PRs are linked. The DevOps unit is the closest analog in the market to a 'full PR state on the card face' pattern — branch + pipeline + approvals + mergeability are all visible without opening the entity. Empty state: the DevOps unit only renders meaningfully when an entity has linked branches/PRs (linkage happens automatically via entity ID matching in branch/PR names through webhooks).
detail_panel: The Entity Detailed View has a dedicated 'DevOps Integrations' section (a first-class tab/block) that appears automatically on Feature, User Story, Task, and Bug views once any branch or MR/PR is linked. The section lists each linked branch with: branch name, source repository, latest pipeline status (and individual job/check results when available via the provider API), and links back to the source DevOps tool. For each linked merge/pull request it shows: PR/MR title, PR number, target branch, author, current approval count vs required, pipeline status, mergeability/conflict status, and a deep link to the PR. Commits can also surface via the older Git commit import integration. Through the 'Customize Entity Detailed View' feature (a layout editor introduced in the v3.13.16 detailed-view-customization beta), the DevOps Integrations block can be added to any entity type beyond the default four, and reordered/sized within the entity layout. Test linkage (Test Cases, Test Plan Runs) appears as a separate Tests-tab section, not inside the DevOps block.
state_coupling: Strong coupling is supported but opt-in via Automation Rules (Custom Business Rules). The DevOps integration ships with an Automation Rules pack that listens for source-control webhook events — branch created, branch pushed, MR/PR opened, MR/PR merged, pipeline status changed — and can trigger Targetprocess state transitions on the linked entity. The canonical examples published by IBM/Targetprocess include: (a) move User Story to 'In Progress' when a branch is created, (b) move User Story to 'In Review' / 'Code Review' when a PR is opened, (c) move User Story to 'Done' or 'Integrated' when the PR is merged to the target branch. Rules are written in JavaScript-like DSL and can be scoped per-project, per-process, per-entity-type, or globally. Granularity supports filtering by repo, target branch, label, approver count, and pipeline status — e.g. 'only transition if PR merged to main AND pipeline succeeded'. Coupling is therefore highly configurable but not enabled by default; the out-of-the-box behavior is purely informational (DevOps section appears, card unit reflects state) with no automatic state change unless an automation rule is installed.
draft_vs_ready_state: [uncertain] Targetprocess documentation describes pipeline status, approval status, and mergeability as the three first-class signals on the DevOps unit, but does not call out a dedicated visual treatment for GitHub/GitLab draft (Work-in-Progress) PRs distinct from ready-for-review PRs. The provider's draft flag is exposed in the underlying API response, so draft state is captured in the data model, but the card-face DevOps unit appears to roll all 'not closed/merged' PRs into the same aggregate calculation regardless of draft status. Automation Rules can be authored to filter on PR draft/ready transitions (e.g. ignore state changes while PR is draft, transition only when ready_for_review fires), but this is custom — not a built-in visual distinction. Confirmation would require direct UI inspection of the DevOps unit against a draft PR.
review_state: Approval state is a first-class card-face element via the DevOps unit's approval icon: gray until the required number of approvals are received, then changes color (green) once the threshold is met. The icon aggregates across multiple linked PRs — if any one of them is still below its required approvals, the unit reflects the unapproved state. In the detail panel's DevOps Integrations section, individual PR rows show approval count (e.g. '1/2 approvals') and the reviewer list when the provider's API exposes it. Requested-but-not-yet-acted reviewers are surfaced through the link back to the source tool rather than as native Targetprocess avatar pills. There is no dedicated 'blocking review' visual on the card face beyond the gray approval icon plus the exclamation mergeability alert when a change-requested review prevents merge.
dod_checklist: DoD is supported as a configuration concept rather than a structured checklist field. Each Work Item type can have a Definition of Done documented per Process via the Process Practices settings, but it is a textual definition for team reference, not an interactive checkable list on the entity. Practical DoD checklists are implemented via: (a) Acceptance Criteria — a rich-text field on User Stories/Features with markdown checkboxes; (b) Personal Tasks / sub-tasks — completed independently and rolled up via effort progress; (c) Custom Fields — boolean or multi-select fields representing DoD gates that can be required for state transition via Custom Business Rules. Custom DoD also has a specific use in the Burndown Visual Report, where teams can define which workflow states count as 'done' for effort calculations. DoD does NOT appear on the card face by default. Completion percentage on cards is driven by effort/story-point rollup, not by DoD checklist completion. No first-class native DoD checklist with template support and gating exists out of the box — it is checklist-by-configuration.
test_linkage: Test linkage is first-class through Targetprocess's native QA / Testing module. Entities: Test Case, Test Plan, Test Plan Run, Test Case Run, with a hierarchical Test Plan structure (since v3.5.0) allowing nested plans. Test Cases link to User Stories and Features via the Test Plan or directly via the Reference field, and a dedicated Tests tab appears on the entity detailed view showing linked Test Cases and their most recent run results (Passed / Failed / Not Run / Blocked / On Hold). Test Plan Runs aggregate results per run. CI/automated test results integrate via the REST API: an external automation suite posts Test Case Run results into Targetprocess, which updates the Test Plan Run roll-up. TestRail integration is also offered as a native option, linking TestRail test cases with Targetprocess user stories via the Reference field. On the card face: no native coverage or pass/fail test badge is included in the DevOps unit. Test result rollup lives only in the detail panel and dedicated QA views, although a custom unit could expose a count if the field is queryable. CI test results (pipeline pass/fail) and functional test results (Test Plan Runs) are conceptually separate fields.
cicd_status: CI/CD pipeline status is part of the DevOps unit on the card face, distinct from PR open/merged status. The pipeline icon reflects the aggregated status across all linked branches/MRs not yet closed/merged — if any one pipeline is failed or in-progress, the card unit shows that state. Supported providers (CI status surfacing): GitLab CI, GitHub Actions/Checks, Azure Pipelines, Bitbucket Pipelines — all via the same DevOps Integrations connector that handles branches/PRs. Visual treatment: a colored icon (green success, red failed, yellow/animated in-progress) plus optional count. Individual check/job names are not enumerated on the card; they are visible in the detail panel's DevOps Integrations section when expanded. A failing pipeline contributes to the mergeability alert (exclamation icon) — so the card communicates 'this story has a quality problem' in two ways: pipeline icon red AND mergeability alert raised. The link from a failing pipeline up to a 'story-level risk' status is not automatic but can be authored via Automation Rules.
release_tagging: Targetprocess uses a first-class Release entity (and Cross-Project Release for portfolio-spanning releases). A Feature, User Story, or Bug belongs to a single Release, which is exposed in the Info panel as the 'Release' field. Hierarchy: Release contains Iterations/Sprints (and Team Iterations for SAFe ART setups); items can also be assigned to a specific Sprint inside the Release. Multi-release membership for a single story is not supported in the standard model — a User Story belongs to one Release at a time (Cross-Project Release wraps multiple project Releases for portfolio visibility but each underlying item still has one release). The Release field can be exposed on the card face as a card unit (configurable via Customize Cards). Build entity is separate and represents a specific built version that can be linked to entities — useful for distinguishing release-target (planned) from delivered-in (actual build). Git tag integration is not first-class as a 'release tag = Targetprocess release' bidirectional binding; the link is via webhook-driven branch/PR linkage rather than tag webhooks specifically.
aggregation: Effort and progress aggregate up the SAFe-style hierarchy automatically (User Story / Task / Bug -> Feature -> Epic -> Portfolio Epic): Total Effort, Effort Remaining, and Effort Completed are calculated bottom-up. The DevOps unit, however, aggregates at the entity level it is configured on — it shows the rolled state of branches/PRs linked to that specific entity by ID. A Feature card can be configured to show its own DevOps unit if PRs are linked directly to the Feature, but Targetprocess does not appear to natively roll up child-story PR state into a parent Feature DevOps indicator (e.g. 'three of five child stories have merged PRs' is not a stock unit). Workarounds exist via Custom Units / Metrics: an admin can define a calculated metric ('count of child user stories where DevOps.PullRequests.AnyMerged = true') and place that metric on the Feature card. This makes Targetprocess one of the few tools where the rollup IS achievable, but it requires explicit metric configuration rather than being a default behavior.
environment_deployment_target: Deployment-environment surfacing is supported through two routes: (a) the Build entity, which represents a specific build/deploy and can be linked to entities, allowing teams to model 'released in build 4.2.1' as a relationship; (b) Automation Rules that listen for deployment webhooks (Azure Pipelines releases, GitHub deployments, GitLab environments, Bitbucket deployments) and update a custom field or move the entity along an 'environment' workflow (Dev / Staging / UAT / Prod). There is no stock 'environment badge' on the card face equivalent to Azure DevOps Boards' deployment pill or Jira Cloud's Deployments column. Teams typically expose deployment state via a custom field ('Deployment Environment' dropdown) populated by automation, then add that field as a card unit. The DevOps unit itself focuses on pre-merge state (branches, PRs, pipelines, approvals) rather than post-merge deployment progression. For RTE-level cross-team visibility, a Visual Report or List view grouping by the deployment-environment custom field is the recommended pattern.
traceability_completeness: Targetprocess is widely cited as one of the better tools for traceability roll-ups — Apptio markets Targetprocess (and Jira Align in the parallel IBM product line) specifically on portfolio-level traceability. The platform supports the data model needed for a composite 'code + tests + DoD + deploy' indicator (DevOps unit for code/PR state; Test Plan Run for tests; custom-field or sub-task for DoD; Build/custom-field for deploy), but it does NOT ship a single first-class composite traceability badge on the card face out of the box. The typical pattern is a custom Metric / Calculated Custom Field that returns true only when all four predicates hold, exposed as a card unit (boolean checkbox icon) or as a column in List view. Visual Reports support traceability matrices (User Story x Test Case x Build x Release) and can be embedded in dashboards. Incomplete traceability does not gate state transitions automatically — gating must be authored via Custom Business Rules (e.g. 'block transition to Done unless DevOps.PullRequests.AllMerged AND TestPlanRun.Status = Passed').
design_pattern: Pattern: full DevOps block on the card face, not a single pill. The DevOps unit is a horizontal cluster of small monochrome icons with color/state encoded per icon — branch icon, pipeline icon (green/red/yellow), approval icon (gray->green), mergeability exclamation (red when blocked). Counts appear inline next to icons when multiple items are linked. State is encoded in BOTH color and icon shape so it is legible without color (an exclamation always means mergeability problem). The pattern is consistent across Story, Feature, Task, and Bug cards because the unit operates on linked branches/PRs by entity ID; the entity TYPE affects whether the section appears by default (yes for Story/Feature/Task/Bug; opt-in for others via customized layout). Empty state when no VCS data is linked: the DevOps unit collapses or is omitted from the rendered card (the unit only materializes when there is data). Card-size discipline: the DevOps unit is configured per card size (XS through XL) — XS cards generally cannot fit it, M/L/XL cards can. This makes Targetprocess the closest market analog to N6's ambition to show full PR state on the card face. The trade-off versus a single composite pill is information density: experienced users can scan four signals at once, but the card surface carries more pixels per item than a Linear/Shortcut compressed-icon approach.
